segments.title: A submarine-heavy fleet turns oil into a strategic objective
segments.summary: The campaign begins with a very large submarine force, weak domestic oil production, and an opponent whose fuel resources offer a tempting strategic objective.
segments.body: The scenario fleet's numerical edge comes mainly from submarines, while its surface force is less dominant. The economy exposes a fuel weakness because Italian oil output per person greatly exceeds Britain's. That difference makes an opponent's oil resources relevant to prewar planning. Domestic oil is best held in reserve while imports remain available, leaving Britain a supply to draw on if overseas access is cut.

evidence.note: The fleet comparison emphasizes submarine strength and contrasts British and Italian oil production.
Domestic fuel reserves are framed as resources to preserve for a future loss of overseas access.

segments.title: Scapa Flow's wartime value and permanent basing are separate questions
segments.summary: Restoring Scapa Flow would turn a useful wartime emergency base into a permanent duty station, with continuing demands on the people assigned there.
segments.body: Scapa Flow may be valuable as an emergency anchorage in wartime without being a good permanent base. The objection concerns keeping personnel stationed there continuously in peacetime. That distinction makes basing policy a question of daily service conditions as well as geography. A strategically useful location can still impose an unattractive long-term posting.

evidence.note: A proposed restoration of Scapa Flow is contrasted with using it only as an emergency wartime naval base.

segments.title: Destroyer refits expose national gun-layout differences
segments.summary: A mass destroyer refit adds twin mounts while prompting a comparison between British, German, and American gun arrangements.
segments.body: Newly available twin turrets raise the destroyer's battery from three to six five-inch guns. The campaign has 293 destroyers, so even a straightforward design change becomes a large modernization programme. The gun arrangement resembles German or American practice more than a characteristically British layout. The final order places 94 destroyers and seven cruisers in refit, an expensive commitment that the campaign economy can still support.

evidence.note: The campaign's large destroyer force is selected for a broad refit.
The six-gun result is compared with British, German, and American destroyer layouts.
The completed orders put 94 destroyers and seven cruisers into an expensive but affordable refit programme.

segments.title: Gibraltar and oil denial shape the plan for war with France
segments.summary: The campaign plan uses Gibraltar to trap opposing ships and targets northern France to disrupt the enemy's oil supply.
segments.body: American ships concentrated in the Mediterranean appear exposed if British control of Gibraltar closes their exit. The strait therefore becomes a tool for containing an opposing fleet. In the planned war with France, northern France is targeted because the scenario locates much of French oil production there. Chokepoint control would trap ships while fuel denial reduced their ability to operate.

evidence.note: Gibraltar is treated as a way to contain hostile ships, while northern France is selected for its oil.
The strategic value of controlling Gibraltar is reiterated.

segments.title: A specialist cruiser substitutes for an inadequate ASW destroyer
segments.summary: A light cruiser is designed around long-range submarine hunting, reconnaissance, speed, and rapid target acquisition rather than heavy firepower.
segments.body: The available destroyer hull cannot carry the desired anti-submarine fit, so the mission moves to a light-cruiser hull. The new ship is assigned long-range ASW and reconnaissance. Reducing speed to 33 knots frees weight for protection, while several rangefinders improve aiming speed. The cruiser has little gun power for its size, but its speed, protection, rangefinders, and ASW equipment suit submarine hunting and fleet screening.

evidence.note: The need for a submarine-hunting escort leads from a destroyer hull to a cruiser hull.
The ship's stated role is long-range ASW and reconnaissance.
Speed is reduced to gain protection, while the finished concept remains fast, under-armed, and rich in rangefinders.

segments.title: The Smoked Haddock class balances torpedoes, armour, and global escort demand
segments.summary: The first ASW cruiser is refined into a 10,000-ton design that can be built in numbers for worldwide duties.
segments.body: Six-inch guns, torpedoes, protection, and displacement compete as the design is brought under 10,000 tons. The final cruiser carries six six-inch guns and torpedoes, with thinner armour accepted to meet the limit. A chat suggestion changes the name from Washington to Smoked Haddock, reserving Washington for the next class. Roughly 60,000 tons of free construction capacity allows six specialist ASW escorts to be ordered for worldwide duties.

evidence.note: Armor, gun caliber, torpedoes, and displacement are traded against one another.
The class is named, identified as a 10,000-ton ASW cruiser, and linked to worldwide fleet duties.
Available construction tonnage supports an initial order for six ships.

segments.title: A super-battleship's secondary battery is built to break the enemy screen
segments.summary: Numerous six-inch guns let a heavily armed battleship engage cruisers and destroyers while its main battery fights capital ships.
segments.body: The ship's nine 16.5-inch guns remain the capital-ship battery. Its unusually numerous six-inch guns have a separate job against cruisers and destroyers supporting the enemy battle line. This lets the battleship challenge the screen meant to offset British battleship superiority in the scenario. Secondary armament therefore serves the fleet's tactical plan as well as the individual ship.

evidence.note: The main and secondary batteries are assigned separate capital-ship and screen-killing purposes.

segments.title: A treaty-survival scenario links ship design to interwar policy
segments.summary: An alternate-history exercise asks how a Washington Treaty-era capital ship and its siblings might survive limitation and serve in the Second World War.
segments.body: The proposed competition would take one of the capital-ship designs sacrificed under the Washington Naval Treaty and give it a plausible alternate history. Entrants would explain why one ship, and perhaps its sisters, survived the treaty system. They would then trace the class into Second World War service and describe the actions it fought. Any answer would have to connect treaty policy and fleet limitation with ship design and wartime employment.

evidence.note: The proposed scenario covers treaty survival, sister ships, Second World War service, and battle history.
The Washington Treaty theme is confirmed as the organizing idea.

segments.title: Submarine concentration changes the balance in the English Channel
segments.summary: A nominally even battleship balance becomes lopsided once more than a hundred British submarines are counted against the French screen.
segments.body: The local order of battle looks balanced when measured only by four battleships on each side. Britain also has 72 coastal and 49 ocean-going submarines in the English Channel area. Those submarines face a French grouping whose surface strength is concentrated in cruisers and destroyers. Counting the undersea force overturns the impression created by capital-ship totals alone.

evidence.note: The English Channel order of battle is compared across battleships, cruisers, destroyers, and submarines.

segments.title: Ballast is the missing control in the game's stability model
segments.summary: A discussion of the updated stability model identifies adjustable ballast as a practical missing tool for correcting ship behavior.
segments.body: The updated game makes pitch and roll more visible constraints when a ship is being designed. A ballast control would provide a direct way to correct those characteristics after choosing the hull, machinery, and fittings. Real ships use ballast as part of trim and stability management. Its absence leaves the player without an equivalent adjustment when the design calculation produces poor behaviour.

evidence.note: The stability update leads directly to a request for player-controlled ship ballasting.

segments.title: Older warships cover distant stations instead of entering reserve
segments.summary: The campaign keeps older ships active on quieter stations while concentrating modern units near Europe and the Mediterranean.
segments.body: Older ships remain active on distant stations where a major war appears less likely. Newer units concentrate around Europe and the Mediterranean, then replace older vessels overseas as more hulls enter service. This avoids maintaining a large mothball fleet while preserving worldwide coverage. The campaign favours rapid, overwhelming wars because a long conflict would disrupt the trade on which Britain's scenario economy depends.

evidence.note: Older ships are assigned to distant, lower-risk stations while newer ships concentrate nearer likely wars.
The active-fleet policy is linked to rapid war termination and protection of a trade-dependent economy.

segments.title: Can a Vauban-style fort anchor a modern city's air defence?
segments.summary: A fixed fort can buy time for mobile defences, provided those mobile systems remain dispersed away from the obvious target.
segments.body: A star fort would be large, visible, and vulnerable to attack. Its purpose would be to provide immediate protection while mobile defences deploy around the city. For a large city, two or three hardened sites could anchor that initial coverage. Mobile systems should remain dispersed elsewhere so a single strike cannot destroy both fixed and deployable layers. A hardened anti-ballistic-missile site is offered as another case in which fixed defences could make an attacker commit to a much larger war.
segments.question: Could a Vauban-style star fort protect a modern city or town from air and missile threats?
segments.answerShort: Potentially. A hardened fort could provide immediate protection and buy time for mobile systems to deploy, while those mobile systems stay dispersed elsewhere.

evidence.note: The audience question is answered by balancing fixed-fort vulnerability against the time it buys mobile defenses.
Hardened defenses are suggested for cities and anti-ballistic-missile facilities.

segments.title: The Washington class becomes a cruiser-sized super destroyer
segments.summary: A second-generation ASW cruiser combines destroyer-like speed and torpedoes with cruiser displacement, protection, and production scale.
segments.body: The Washington design expands the first ASW cruiser into a roughly 12,000-ton ship with the speed and torpedoes of a large destroyer. Eight six-inch guns, eight three-inch guns, and two quadruple torpedo launchers give it enough firepower to fight surface screens as well as submarines. Maximum bulkheads, long range, 35-knot speed, and the available armour support survivability and sustained operations. With roughly 120,000 tons of construction capacity free, ten ships fit the programme while an eleventh would exceed the limit by about 6,000 tons.

evidence.note: The new ASW cruiser gains torpedoes and is described as a large or cruiser-sized destroyer.
Speed, armor, bulkheads, range, armament, and bridge style are refined into the Washington class.
Available construction tonnage is converted into a production estimate for the class.

segments.title: Deployed warships can signal political commitment
segments.summary: Ship size can advertise the strength of a state's commitment, though the game cannot reproduce the diplomatic influence that a real deployment might exert.
segments.body: Naval presence is treated as a political signal, with larger vessels showing a stronger level of interest. Different force packages can therefore communicate different degrees of commitment. The game models fleet movement without allowing those deployments to influence another state's decisions. That limitation separates moving ships on a map from the diplomatic effects their presence may create.

evidence.note: An aside links larger deployed vessels with a stronger level of interest and notes that UAD cannot model influence over another state's decisions.

segments.title: Deliberate force mismatches overwhelm enemy destroyers and cruisers
segments.summary: The campaign doctrine answers destroyers with light cruisers and enemy cruisers or battlecruisers with a mass of battleships.
segments.body: The fleet plan assigns light cruisers to enemy destroyers and masses battleships against cruisers or battlecruisers. Each matchup seeks a local class advantage instead of mirroring the opposing formation. Light cruisers provide the answer to hostile screening forces, while battleships overmatch the heavier ships behind them. This doctrine explains the campaign's large orders for both classes.

evidence.note: The fleet doctrine explicitly pairs light cruisers against destroyers and battleships against cruisers and battlecruisers.

segments.title: How fast should a 257,000-horsepower light cruiser be?
segments.summary: A light cruiser with 257,000 shaft horsepower should exceed 40 knots unless inefficient propellers waste the available power.
segments.body: Installed power gives a rough speed expectation, though propeller efficiency could still waste some of it. A light cruiser with 257,000 shaft horsepower is estimated to exceed 40 knots. The reported game design reaches 42.9 knots. That figure matches its assigned purpose of overtaking destroyers.
segments.question: What speed would a light cruiser with 257,000 shaft horsepower be expected to reach?
segments.answerShort: More than 40 knots with reasonable propellers; the reported design reaches 42.9 knots and is intended to catch destroyers.

evidence.note: The cruiser power figure prompts a speed estimate above 40 knots with a propeller-efficiency caveat.
The final reported speed is 42.9 knots, with destroyer pursuit given as the design purpose.

segments.title: Port deployments close both ends of the English Channel
segments.summary: Reinforcements, mine-sweeping capacity, reconnaissance, and port control are combined to blockade the English Channel before war with France.
segments.body: New light cruisers reinforce the main fleet as tension with France rises. Minesweeping capacity, reconnaissance, supply, and control radius are checked alongside ship numbers. A Portsmouth formation covers one end of the English Channel, while ships at Dover move to close the other. Within the scenario, port placement and local support turn the Channel into an operational barrier.

evidence.note: Ships reinforce the English Channel fleet and the local formation's sweeping, reconnaissance, and control values are reviewed.
Port-based formations are positioned to block both ends of the Channel against France.

segments.title: Runway aircraft do not become carrier aircraft by relocation
segments.summary: CATOBAR operations impose design requirements that ordinary runway aircraft cannot satisfy without substantial changes.
segments.body: CATOBAR operation requires an aircraft designed for it, and ordinary runway suitability is insufficient. The F-35A, F-35B, and F-35C show how different operating methods produce distinct variants. Eurofighter never became a CATOBAR aircraft, so moving it to such a carrier would not make it suitable for deck operations. Carrier compatibility has to be part of the aircraft's design.

evidence.note: CATOBAR aircraft are distinguished from ordinary runway aircraft through the F-35 variants and Eurofighter example.

segments.title: Improved oil burners create a fleet-wide refit burden
segments.summary: A new propulsion upgrade promises better performance while requiring every existing ship design to be revisited.
segments.body: An improved fuel-oil burner immediately creates a plan to revisit every ship design in the fleet. Better machinery means a large refit burden once hundreds of active vessels are considered. The campaign postpones that work to a later session because each existing design must be updated. A single propulsion advance can therefore create a fleet-wide standardization programme.

evidence.note: Improved fuel-oil burners are treated as a major upgrade that must be applied across every existing ship design.
